sections.title: Introduction
sections.text:
Welcome. Today we follow one of the most remarkable lives in history: the apostle Paul. He started out as the fiercest enemy of the early church, and he became its greatest missionary. He traveled thousands of miles by foot and by ship, started churches across the Roman world, and wrote thirteen letters that are now part of our New Testament.

His story is told in the book of Acts, from chapter nine to the end. As you listen, think about this: if God could change a man like Saul, is there anyone He can't change — including you?

sections.title: The Story, Part 1
sections.text:
Saul was born in Tarsus and trained as a strict Pharisee. He was zealous for God, but he believed the followers of Jesus were dangerous, so he set out to destroy the church. He went from house to house, dragging men and women off to prison. He even got letters from the high priest so he could arrest believers in the city of Damascus.

But on the road, everything changed. Acts chapter nine, verses three and four: “And as he journeyed, he came near Damascus: and suddenly there shined round about him a light from heaven: And he fell to the earth, and heard a voice saying unto him, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?” Saul asked, “Who art thou, Lord?” And the answer came: “I am Jesus whom thou persecutest.”

When Saul got up, he was blind. His companions led him by the hand into Damascus, and for three days he didn't eat or drink. Then God spoke to a disciple named Ananias and told him to go to Saul. Ananias was afraid — he knew Saul's reputation! But God said, “he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel.” So Ananias went, laid his hands on Saul, and called him “Brother Saul.” Something like scales fell from Saul's eyes, and he could see again. He was baptized, and right away he began preaching in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God.

At first, the believers were afraid of him. But a man named Barnabas, whose name means son of consolation or encouragement, took Saul and vouched for him. Later, in the church at Antioch, the Holy Ghost said, “Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them.” From this point on, Acts calls him by his Roman name, Paul.

sections.title: The Story, Part 2
sections.text:
On his first missionary journey, Paul traveled with Barnabas to the island of Cyprus and then to cities in the region of Galatia, in what is now Turkey. Many people believed, both Jews and Gentiles. But Paul also faced fierce opposition. In the city of Lystra, he was stoned and dragged out of the city, and left for dead. But when the believers gathered around him, he got up — and the next day he went on to the next town.

On his second journey, Paul traveled with Silas, and a young believer named Timothy joined them. In a vision, Paul saw a man of Macedonia pleading, “Come over into Macedonia, and help us.” So for the first time, the gospel crossed into Europe. In the city of Philippi, a businesswoman named Lydia, a seller of purple cloth, believed and opened her home to them.

But in Philippi, Paul and Silas were also beaten and thrown into the inner prison, with their feet fastened in stocks. And what did they do? Acts chapter sixteen, verse twenty-five: “And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them.” Suddenly there was a great earthquake. The prison doors flew open, and everyone's chains came loose. The jailer, thinking the prisoners had escaped, was about to kill himself. But Paul shouted, “Do thyself no harm: for we are all here.” Trembling, the jailer asked, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” And they answered, “Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house.” That very night, the jailer and his whole household were baptized.

Paul went on to Thessalonica, Berea, Athens, and Corinth, where he stayed a year and a half. On his third journey, he spent about three years in Ephesus, teaching daily. Wherever he went, he preached Jesus, and churches were born.

Eventually Paul returned to Jerusalem, where he was arrested after a riot. He spent two years as a prisoner in Caesarea. As a Roman citizen, he appealed to Caesar, and he was sent by ship to Rome. On the way, a terrible storm raged for fourteen days, and the ship was wrecked. But God had promised that no one would be lost, and all two hundred and seventy-six people on board made it safely to the island of Melita. Finally Paul reached Rome. Acts ends with him living there for two whole years under guard, welcoming everyone who came to him, and preaching the kingdom of God with all confidence.

sections.title: The Lesson
sections.text:
What can we learn from Paul's life?

First, no one is beyond the reach of God's grace. Paul once called himself the chief of sinners. If Jesus could turn Saul the persecutor into Paul the apostle, He can change anyone.

Second, we all need a Barnabas, and we can all be one. Ananias and Barnabas took a risk on Saul when others were afraid. Who could you encourage or welcome today?

Third, joy doesn't depend on circumstances. Paul and Silas sang hymns at midnight in a prison cell. Later, from another prison, Paul wrote to the Philippians, “I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.” Our strength comes from Christ, not from our situation.

And finally, finish the race. Near the end of his life, Paul wrote to Timothy: “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith.” Through beatings, shipwrecks, and prisons, he kept going. God gives us the strength to keep going too.

sections.title: Prayer and Reflection
sections.text:
Who is someone you've thought was too far from God to ever change? Pray for them now. And think of one person you could encourage this week, the way Barnabas encouraged Paul.

Let's pray. Lord Jesus, thank You that Your grace reached Paul, and that it reaches me. Make me an encourager like Barnabas. Give me joy that doesn't depend on my circumstances, and strength to keep the faith until I finish my course. In Your name, Amen.

Thank you for listening. You've now heard all thirteen stories. Go back and listen to your favorites anytime, and keep growing in God's word.
